script.title: How to Make a Budget That Actually Works (Step by Step for Beginners)
script.hook: Most budgets fail by week 3. This one uses 4 numbers, and we'll build it live on a $3,200 paycheck.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: Most budgets fail by week three. Not because people are bad with money, but because the budget was built like a tax form: forty categories, a spreadsheet with colors, and a plan that falls apart the first time you buy lunch. Today we're building a budget the other way. Four numbers. It takes about twenty minutes, and we'll build it live on a real-looking example: a take-home pay of thirty-two hundred dollars a month. By the end, you'll know exactly what you can spend this week without guessing, and you'll have a ten-minute weekly habit that keeps it working. Grab your banking app and a note on your phone. You'll want your own numbers ready as we go. And quick note: the person in this example is fictional, so swap in your own figures as we go.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. the small round green piggy bank mascot with big eyes holding a small notepad with four empty boxes, cheerful. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Why most budgets fail
segments.narration: Here's what usually goes wrong. People start with what they wish they spent, not what they actually spend. They write down two hundred dollars for food when the real number is four hundred and fifty, and by the middle of the month the budget is already broken. Then they feel guilty, stop opening the spreadsheet, and the whole thing quietly dies. The second problem is too much detail. If you have separate lines for coffee, lunch, snacks and takeout, every purchase becomes a decision about which box it goes in. That's exhausting. A budget only works if it's easier to follow than to ignore. So our rules are simple. Start with real numbers from your last month. Use as few categories as possible. And make the most important parts automatic, so they happen even when you're busy or tired.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a tangled spreadsheet with too many boxes next to a calm simple list. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 1: your real take-home pay
segments.narration: Step one is the number that actually lands in your account. Not your salary. Your take-home pay, after taxes, retirement contributions and health insurance come out. Open your banking app and look at your last two paychecks. If you're paid every two weeks, add two paychecks together and that's your normal month. Some months you'll get three paychecks. Don't build your budget on those. Treat the third paycheck as a bonus you'll give a job when it arrives. If your income changes month to month, from tips, gigs or commissions, use your lowest month from the past six months as your budget number. Anything above that is extra. For our example, the take-home is thirty-two hundred dollars a month. That's the only income number we'll use from here on.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a paycheck envelope with a smaller amount sliding out of it, the small round green piggy bank mascot with big eyes pointing at it. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 2: the bills that must get paid
segments.narration: Step two: list every bill that has to get paid no matter what. Rent, utilities, phone, insurance, transportation, minimum debt payments, and groceries. Yes, groceries go here, because you have to eat. Pull the real numbers from last month's statement. In our example, rent is twelve hundred and fifty. Utilities and phone are one sixty. Insurance is one twenty. The car and gas come to two twenty. Groceries are four hundred. The student loan payment is one eighty. And subscriptions are forty-five. Add it up and you get two thousand three hundred and seventy-five dollars. That's number one: essentials. While you're in your statements, check the subscriptions line. Most people find at least one they forgot they had. Cancel it now, while you're thinking about it, not later.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a short stack of bills with a house, a lightbulb and a shopping basket icon. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 3: pay yourself first
segments.narration: Step three is the one most budgets skip. Before you spend anything on fun, decide what goes to savings, and make it automatic. In our example, three hundred dollars a month goes to savings, split across the two paychecks, so a hundred and fifty each payday. Schedule the transfer for the day after payday, not the same day, so a late deposit never bounces it. If three hundred feels impossible right now, start with twenty-five. The amount matters less than the habit. Where does it go? If you don't have an emergency fund yet, this is it. Start with a goal of one thousand dollars, then build toward a few months of essentials. If your job offers a 401(k) match, make sure you're getting the full match too, because that's money you'd otherwise leave on the table. That's number two: savings, three hundred.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. the small round green piggy bank mascot with big eyes dropping coins into a jar labelled with a small arrow, morning sun. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 4: sinking funds for the expenses you forget
segments.narration: Step four fixes the thing that breaks most budgets in month two: expenses that don't come every month. Car repairs. Birthdays and holidays. The annual software subscription. The dentist. They feel like surprises, but they're not. They're just on a different calendar. So we set aside a little every month for them. That's called a sinking fund. Here's how. Write down every irregular expense you can remember from the last year and roughly what it cost. Add it up and divide by twelve. In our example, the car needs about six hundred a year in repairs and maintenance, and gifts are about six hundred. That's twelve hundred a year, so one hundred dollars a month. Move it to a separate savings account, or a labelled bucket if your bank offers them. That's number three: sinking funds, one hundred.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a calendar with a few circled dates and small labelled jars beneath it. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 5: the number you can actually spend
segments.narration: Now the best part. Take your income and subtract the first three numbers. Thirty-two hundred, minus twenty-three seventy-five in essentials, minus three hundred in savings, minus one hundred in sinking funds. That leaves four hundred and twenty-five dollars. That's number four: your flexible spending. Eating out, clothes, hobbies, a night out, the random stuff. The magic here is that this number is guilt-free. Your bills are covered. Your savings already happened. Your irregular costs are handled. So anything inside the four twenty-five is yours to spend however you want, without a spreadsheet and without guilt. Now divide it by four and a bit. That's roughly a hundred dollars a week. If you remember only one number from this budget, make it this one. A hundred a week. You'll check it every Sunday.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. the small round green piggy bank mascot with big eyes relaxing in a café with a small coffee, a weekly calendar beside it. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: What if the numbers don't work?
segments.narration: Sometimes you do the math and the last number is negative. Essentials plus savings are already more than you bring home. That's not a failure. That's information, and it's the most useful thing a budget can tell you. Here's the order to fix it. First, look at the big three: housing, transportation and food. That's where most of the money goes, and small changes there beat cutting every coffee. Can you cook four more dinners a month? Refinance the car? Get a roommate at your next lease? Second, call your providers. Phone, internet and insurance can often be lowered just by asking or shopping around. Third, if you're still short, lower savings temporarily to twenty-five dollars, but keep the transfer running. And if your income simply doesn't cover essentials, the answer is earning more, not budgeting harder.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a balance scale with a house, a car and a grocery bag on one side. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Make it automatic
segments.narration: A budget you have to remember to follow won't survive a busy month. So let's automate it. Set your bills to autopay from checking, at least the minimum on every card and loan, so you never pay a late fee. Schedule your savings transfer for the day after each payday. Schedule your sinking fund transfer the same way. Now your checking account has one job: hold your bills and your weekly spending money. Some people go one step further and move the flexible money to a separate account or a debit card with a weekly top-up. That way the balance you see is exactly what you can spend. You don't need an app for any of this. Your bank's built-in scheduled transfers do the job for free. If you do like apps, we compared the popular budgeting apps on our site, linked below.
segments.on_screen_text: Bills, savings, sinking funds: all automatic
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. three small pipes carrying coins from one big tank into three smaller tanks. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The 10-minute Sunday check-in
segments.narration: Here's the habit that keeps the whole thing alive: a ten-minute money check-in once a week. Same day, same time. Sunday evening works for most people. Open your bank app and look at three things. One: how much of this week's hundred dollars did you spend? Two: did any bill or subscription surprise you? Three: what's coming up next week that needs money, like a birthday or a car registration? That's it. If you went over this week, you don't need to feel bad. Just spend a little less next week. If you came in under, let it roll over or move it to savings. Once a month, add five minutes to update your sinking funds and check that every automatic transfer actually ran. This tiny habit is the difference between a budget that lasts a month and one that lasts for years.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. the small round green piggy bank mascot with big eyes on a sofa with a phone and a cup of tea, a small checklist of three items. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Common mistakes
segments.narration: A few mistakes to avoid. Mistake one: budgeting your salary instead of take-home pay. Always use what actually lands. Mistake two: forgetting irregular expenses. That's what sinking funds fix. Mistake three: no money for fun. If your budget has zero flexible spending, you'll break it, so keep at least a small amount that's guilt-free. Mistake four: quitting after one bad week. Everyone overspends sometimes. A budget isn't a test you pass or fail. It's a plan you adjust. And mistake five: tracking every dollar forever. Tracking for one month is great for learning where your money goes, but after that, the automatic system does most of the work. You only need to watch your weekly number.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. five small warning signs along a winding path, the small round green piggy bank mascot with big eyes stepping around them. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Let's recap. One: find your real take-home pay. In our example, thirty-two hundred. Two: list your essential bills from real statements. Twenty-three seventy-five. Three: pay yourself first, automatically. Three hundred. Four: add sinking funds for the expenses you forget. One hundred. What's left is your guilt-free spending, four twenty-five a month, about a hundred a week. Then automate everything and check in for ten minutes every Sunday. If you want help doing this with your own numbers, the free seven-day money reset in the description walks you through it one small step a day. And if you want to see what this budget looks like at your exact salary, we've got example budgets for different incomes on our site. Links are below.

script.title: Debt Snowball vs Avalanche: We Ran the Real Numbers
script.hook: Snowball or avalanche? We ran both on $7,800 of debt. One saves $327. The other wins 14 months sooner.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: Snowball or avalanche? They're the two most popular ways to pay off debt, and people argue about them constantly. So instead of arguing, we ran both, month by month, on the exact same debt. Three debts, seventy-eight hundred dollars in total, and four hundred dollars a month to throw at them. One method saved three hundred and twenty-seven dollars in interest. The other gave the first win fourteen months sooner. By the end of this video you'll know exactly how each one works, what the real difference is, and how to pick the one you'll actually stick with, because the best payoff plan is the one you don't quit. The example is fictional, but the math is real, and you can rerun it with your own numbers using the free calculator linked below.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. two paths up a small hill, one with a snowball, one with a gentle rockslide. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The example debts
segments.narration: Here's our example. Debt one: a credit card with forty-five hundred dollars at twenty-four percent APR, with a minimum payment of one thirty-five. Debt two: a store card with eight hundred dollars at eighteen percent, minimum thirty. Debt three: a personal loan with twenty-five hundred dollars at ten percent, minimum eighty. Add up the minimums and you get two forty-five a month. Our example person can afford four hundred a month for debt. So every month, they pay every minimum, and the extra one fifty-five goes to one target debt. When that debt is gone, its minimum rolls into the next target. That rolling is what makes both methods work. The only difference between snowball and avalanche is which debt gets the extra money first.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. three stacked cards of different sizes with small percent signs. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: How the snowball works
segments.narration: The debt snowball targets the smallest balance first, no matter the interest rate. In our example, that's the eight hundred dollar store card. All the extra money goes there. Because the balance is small, it disappears fast: paid off in month five. Then that thirty dollar minimum plus the extra rolls onto the next smallest, the personal loan, which is gone by month fourteen. Then everything piles onto the big credit card, which is paid off in month twenty-four. Total interest paid: about seventeen hundred and ninety-two dollars. The point of the snowball isn't math. It's motivation. You see a debt disappear in five months, you feel progress, and that feeling keeps you going. For a lot of people, especially if you've tried and quit before, that early win matters more than anything.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a small snowball rolling downhill and growing, the small round green piggy bank mascot with big eyes cheering. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: How the avalanche works
segments.narration: The debt avalanche targets the highest interest rate first. In our example, that's the twenty-four percent credit card. It's also the biggest balance, so it takes a while: it's paid off in month nineteen. Then the money rolls to the eighteen percent store card, gone in month twenty-one, and finally the ten percent loan, done in month twenty-four. Total interest paid: about fourteen hundred and sixty-five dollars. Same finish line, month twenty-four, but three hundred and twenty-seven dollars less in interest. The avalanche always costs the least, because every extra dollar goes to the debt that's costing you the most. The tradeoff is that your first win can take a long time. In our example, nineteen months with no debt fully gone. That's where people sometimes lose motivation.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a gentle cascade of coins knocking down the tallest block first. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Side by side
segments.narration: So here they are side by side. Snowball: first debt gone in month five, debt-free in month twenty-four, about seventeen ninety-two in interest. Avalanche: first debt gone in month nineteen, debt-free in month twenty-four, about fourteen sixty-five in interest. The difference is three hundred and twenty-seven dollars over two years, about fourteen dollars a month. That's real money, but it's probably smaller than you expected. And here's the thing the debate usually misses. Both of these beat the default, which is paying minimums and spending whatever's left. The biggest decision isn't snowball versus avalanche. It's deciding on a fixed monthly debt number, and sticking to it every single month. Picking either method and following it is the win.
segments.on_screen_text: Avalanche saves $327. Snowball wins 14 months sooner.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a simple two-column chart with two bars of slightly different heights. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: When the difference gets big
segments.narration: The gap between the two methods grows in a few situations. One: when there's a big difference in interest rates, like a thirty percent card and a five percent car loan. Two: when the high-rate debt is also large. Three: when the payoff takes many years. In those cases, snowball can cost you thousands more, not hundreds. On the other hand, if all your debts have similar rates, the difference almost disappears, and you might as well take the motivation of the snowball. So before you choose, run your own numbers. Put your balances, rates and monthly amount into the free debt payoff calculator linked below. It'll show you both methods with your real debts in about a minute. If the gap is small, choose snowball. If it's large, think hard about avalanche.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a tall stack of coins next to a short stack, a magnifying glass between them. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Which one should you pick?
segments.narration: Here's a simple way to decide. Pick snowball if you've tried paying off debt before and stopped, if you have several small balances you could knock out quickly, or if seeing progress is what keeps you motivated. Pick avalanche if you're a numbers person who stays motivated by a spreadsheet, if you have a high-rate debt that's clearly costing you the most, or if the calculator shows a big gap. And if you're not sure, there's a hybrid. Knock out one tiny debt first for a quick win, something you can clear in a month or two. Then switch to avalanche for everything else. You get the early motivation and most of the savings. There's no wrong answer here, as long as the extra payment keeps happening every month.
segments.on_screen_text: Pick the one you'll stick to
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. the small round green piggy bank mascot with big eyes at a fork in a path, holding a small compass. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Make either method faster
segments.narration: Whichever you choose, here's how to speed it up. First, lower the rates. Call your card company and ask for a lower APR. It takes a few minutes, and sometimes it works. If you have good credit, a zero percent balance transfer card can pause interest for a year or more, though most charge a three to five percent fee. Check that the fee is smaller than the interest you'd save, and that you can pay it off before the promo ends. We compare balance transfer cards on our site. Second, find extra money. Every raise, tax refund or side income can go straight to your target debt. Even an extra fifty dollars a month shortens the timeline noticeably. Third, stop adding new debt. Take the card out of your phone's wallet until you're done.
segments.on_screen_text: Lower the rate. Add extra. Stop new debt.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a phone with a card being removed from it, coins flowing to a target. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Protect your plan
segments.narration: One more thing before you start: keep a small emergency buffer. If your car breaks down and you have zero savings, that repair goes right back on the credit card, and it feels like all your progress just vanished. So before going all-in on debt, build a starter emergency fund of five hundred to a thousand dollars. It's not exciting, but it's what keeps one bad week from undoing six months of work. Then automate your minimum payments so you never pay a late fee or take a credit score hit, and set up the extra payment to go out automatically, right after payday. Finally, write down your debt-free date and put it somewhere you'll see it. Watching that date get closer is surprisingly powerful.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a small umbrella sheltering a jar of coins from rain. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Let's recap. Both methods pay every minimum, put extra money on one target debt, and roll payments forward as each debt disappears. Snowball targets the smallest balance first, for faster wins. Avalanche targets the highest rate first, for the lowest total interest. In our fictional example with seventy-eight hundred dollars of debt and four hundred a month, avalanche saved three hundred and twenty-seven dollars, and snowball cleared the first debt fourteen months sooner. Both finished in month twenty-four. Run your own numbers, choose the method you'll stick with, keep a starter emergency fund, and automate the payments. The free debt payoff guide and calculator are linked in the description, along with our balance transfer comparison.

script.title: How to Build an Emergency Fund (Even on a Tight Budget)
script.hook: $1,000 is the first goal. Then 3 months of essentials. Here's how to get there on a tight budget.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: An emergency fund is the most boring thing in personal finance, and it's also the one that changes your life the most. It's the difference between a car repair being an annoying week and a car repair being three months of credit card debt. In this video we'll cover how much you actually need, using simple math, where to keep it so it's safe and still earns something, how to build it even when money is tight, and the rules for when to use it. We'll start with a first goal of one thousand dollars, and then build toward three to six months of essential expenses. We'll use a fictional example with two thousand dollars a month in essentials, so you can follow the math with your own numbers.
segments.on_screen_text: The boring account that changes everything
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. the small round green piggy bank mascot with big eyes holding a small umbrella over a jar of coins. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: What an emergency fund is for
segments.narration: An emergency fund is money you set aside for things that are urgent, necessary and unexpected. Your car breaks down and you need it for work. You lose your job or your hours get cut. A medical bill you didn't see coming. Your phone dies and you need one to work. What it's not for: a sale, a vacation, or holiday gifts. Those are planned expenses, and they belong in sinking funds, which we cover in another video. The point of the emergency fund is to break the cycle where every surprise goes on a credit card. Once you have it, an emergency becomes a transfer instead of a crisis. And there's a real mental health benefit too. Knowing you have a cushion makes every other money decision calmer.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a toolbox, a medical cross and a car wrench next to a small safe. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Goal one: a starter fund
segments.narration: Your first goal is a starter emergency fund of five hundred to one thousand dollars. That covers a lot of the most common surprises, like a car repair, a vet visit or an urgent trip. If you have high-interest credit card debt, this is where you pause the emergency fund and switch to paying down debt, because a twenty-four percent card costs more than your savings will earn. But don't skip the starter fund. Without it, any surprise goes back on the card and undoes your debt progress. How fast can you get there? At fifty dollars a week, you hit a thousand in about twenty weeks, roughly five months. At twenty-five a week, about ten months. Pick a number that works, automate it, and let it run.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a small piggy bank filling up, a progress bar beside it. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Goal two: how much you really need
segments.narration: Once your high-interest debt is under control, the next goal is three to six months of essential expenses. Notice it's essentials, not your full income. Rent, utilities, groceries, insurance, transportation, minimum debt payments, phone. In our example, that's two thousand dollars a month. So three months is six thousand dollars, and six months is twelve thousand. Which end should you aim for? Lean toward three months if you have a stable job, two incomes in the household, and no dependents. Lean toward six months or more if you're self-employed, work on commission, are the only income for your household, or work in an industry with frequent layoffs. If six thousand sounds huge, remember you're not doing it this month. You're building it a little every payday.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a row of six small calendars, three of them highlighted. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Where to keep it
segments.narration: Where you keep your emergency fund matters. It needs to be safe, separate and accessible. Safe means a federally insured account. At a bank, that's FDIC insurance, and at a credit union, it's NCUA insurance, generally up to two hundred and fifty thousand dollars per depositor, per institution, per ownership category. Separate means not in your checking account, where it's too easy to spend by accident. Accessible means you can get to it within a day or two. Not invested in the stock market, because emergencies often happen when markets are down. For most people, a high-yield savings account at an insured bank is the best home. It pays much more than a typical savings account, and you can still transfer money out quickly. We compare high-yield savings accounts on our site, linked below.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a small vault with a shield icon, connected to a phone by a dotted line. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: How to build it on a tight budget
segments.narration: What if your budget feels like it has nothing left? Here are four ways to find the money. One: start embarrassingly small. Ten or twenty dollars per paycheck, scheduled automatically. Small amounts build the habit, and the habit is what grows. Two: use windfalls. A tax refund, a bonus, a birthday check, or money from selling things you don't use. Put at least half straight into the fund. Three: cancel one subscription and redirect it. If you cut a fifteen dollar streaming service, set up a fifteen dollar transfer the same day, so the money doesn't just disappear into spending. Four: when you pay off a debt, keep paying it to yourself. That car payment or card minimum you're used to sending out can now go into savings. You won't miss money you were already living without.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. four small coin streams flowing into one jar. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Make it automatic
segments.narration: The single best thing you can do is make it automatic. In your bank app, set a recurring transfer from checking to your emergency savings for the day after each payday. The day after, so a late paycheck doesn't cause an overdraft. Then, and this is important, don't link a debit card to that savings account, and don't keep it on your home screen. A little friction helps. Some people even keep their emergency fund at a different bank from their checking, so it takes a day to move money. That one-day delay is enough to stop impulse spending, but still fast enough for a real emergency. Set it up once and you never have to think about it again. Check it at your monthly money check-in to make sure it's still running.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a small conveyor belt carrying coins from one building to another. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: When to use it, and how to refill it
segments.narration: When something happens, ask three questions. Is it urgent? Is it necessary? Is it unexpected? If the answer to all three is yes, use the fund without guilt. That's exactly what it's for. People sometimes put an emergency on a credit card to protect their savings, and then pay interest on it for months. Don't do that. The money is there to be used. After you use it, pause any extra goals and refill the fund first. If you spent eight hundred dollars, set a plan to rebuild it over the next few months, maybe by temporarily redirecting your flexible spending. And if something isn't an emergency but you still want it, like a trip or a new laptop, that's a sinking fund goal. Start saving for it separately.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a checklist with three ticks next to an open jar. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Common mistakes
segments.narration: A few common mistakes. Keeping it in checking, where it slowly gets spent. Investing it in stocks or crypto, where it might be down twenty percent the day you need it. Waiting to start until you can save a big amount. Using it for planned expenses like holidays, and then having nothing when the real emergency comes. And the opposite mistake: holding so much in emergency savings that you skip your 401(k) match or keep high-interest debt around. Once you're past six months or so, extra cash usually works harder somewhere else. And make sure it's actually insured. Some apps hold money through partner banks, and the details matter. We wrote a guide on checking if your savings app is FDIC insured, linked below.

segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a few small warning signs next to a calm savings jar. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Let's recap. An emergency fund is for things that are urgent, necessary and unexpected. Start with five hundred to a thousand dollars. Then, once high-interest debt is handled, build toward three to six months of essential expenses. In our example, that's six to twelve thousand dollars. Keep it in an insured, separate, accessible account, like a high-yield savings account. Automate a transfer the day after every payday, even if it's small, and add windfalls. Use it without guilt when you need it, then refill it first. It's boring. It works. script.title: How Credit Scores Actually Work (and How to Raise Yours)
script.hook: 5 factors make up your credit score, and 2 of them are 65% of it. Here's what actually moves the number.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: Your credit score affects your apartment application, your car loan rate, your insurance in many states, and sometimes even your phone plan. But most people have no idea how it's calculated, so they worry about the wrong things. In this video we'll go through the five factors that make up a FICO score, the score most lenders use, and how much each one counts. Two of them make up sixty-five percent of the score, and those are where you should spend your energy. Then we'll cover how to build credit from zero, how to recover from mistakes, and how to check and fix your credit report for free. No paid services needed. Everything here you can do yourself in an afternoon.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. the small round green piggy bank mascot with big eyes looking at a simple gauge dial with a needle pointing upward. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Score vs report
segments.narration: First, a quick difference that confuses a lot of people. Your credit report is the record: every account you have, your balances, your payment history, and any collections. It's kept by three credit bureaus, Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. Your credit score is a number calculated from that report. FICO scores and VantageScore are the two main brands, and most FICO scores run from three hundred to eight fifty. Because there are three bureaus and several scoring models, you actually have many scores, and they won't match exactly. That's normal. What matters is the trend and the range, not the exact number. And checking your own score or report is a soft inquiry. It never hurts your score, so check as often as you want.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a folder of papers next to a single number badge. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Factor 1: payment history (35%)
segments.narration: The biggest factor is payment history, about thirty-five percent of a FICO score. Simply put: do you pay on time? One late payment can hurt a lot, especially if your score is high. But here's an important detail. Lenders generally don't report a payment as late to the credit bureaus until it's at least thirty days past due. So if you miss a due date by a few days, pay it immediately. You'll probably owe a late fee, but it may never show up on your report. The fix for this factor is simple: set up autopay for at least the minimum payment on every card and loan. You can always pay more manually. Autopay just makes sure you never miss. That one setting protects the biggest part of your score.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a calendar with every date checked off, the small round green piggy bank mascot with big eyes giving a thumbs up. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Factor 2: amounts owed (30%)
segments.narration: The second biggest factor is amounts owed, about thirty percent. The key idea here is credit utilization: how much of your available credit card limit you're using. If you have a thousand dollar limit and a three hundred dollar balance, your utilization is thirty percent. A common guideline is to keep it under thirty percent, and people with the highest scores often stay under ten. Here's what most people don't know: utilization is usually based on the balance your card reports, which is often your statement balance, even if you pay in full every month. So if you want a lower reported balance before applying for a loan, pay the card down before the statement closes. And unlike late payments, utilization has no long memory. Pay it down, and your score can recover quickly.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a credit card next to a simple bar filled one third of the way. No text, no logos, no real people.

chart.title: What a FICO score is made of

segments.heading: Factors 3 to 5
segments.narration: The last three factors are smaller. Length of credit history is about fifteen percent: how old your accounts are on average, and how long since your oldest account was opened. That's why closing your oldest card can sometimes hurt a little. New credit is about ten percent: recent applications and hard inquiries. For most people, one hard inquiry drops a score by less than five points, and it only counts in FICO scores for twelve months. Credit mix is the last ten percent: having different kinds of credit, like a card and an installment loan. You should never take out a loan just to improve your mix. These factors matter, but they move slowly. Focus on the big two, paying on time and keeping balances low, and these mostly take care of themselves.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. three small blocks of different heights beside two tall blocks. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Building credit from zero
segments.narration: If you have no credit history at all, you're not bad with credit. You're just invisible to the scoring models. Here are the common ways to start. A secured credit card: you put down a deposit, often a couple hundred dollars, and that becomes your limit. Use it for one small bill, like a streaming subscription, set it to autopay in full, and never carry a balance. A credit-builder loan: you make monthly payments into a locked account, and the lender reports those payments. At the end, you get the money back, minus any interest and fees. Being added as an authorized user on a family member's card with a long, clean history can also help, as long as they pay on time. Most people can build a FICO score within about six months of activity.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a tiny sprout growing out of a credit card shaped plant pot. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recovering from mistakes
segments.narration: If your credit has taken some hits, the good news is that time is on your side. Most negative items, like late payments and collections, can stay on your report for up to seven years, but their impact fades much sooner as you add on-time history. Here's the recovery order. One: get current on everything. Stop new late payments first. Two: pay down card balances to lower utilization. That's the fastest lever you have. Three: don't close old accounts unless they have an annual fee you can't justify. Four: be careful with anyone who promises to remove accurate negative information for a fee. The FTC warns about credit repair scams. Anything a credit repair company can legally do, like disputing errors, you can do yourself, free.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a path going uphill with small flags marking steps. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Check and dispute your report free
segments.narration: Check your credit report from all three bureaus for free at AnnualCreditReport dot com. That's the official site, and you can now get free reports weekly. Look for accounts you don't recognize, late payments you know you made on time, wrong balances, or old debts that should have aged off. Errors are more common than you'd think. If you find one, file a dispute directly with the bureau that shows it. You can do it online. Explain what's wrong and include copies of any proof, like a bank statement showing the payment. The bureau generally has thirty days to investigate. And if you see accounts you didn't open, that could be identity theft. Report it at IdentityTheft dot gov and consider freezing your credit. We have a whole video on that.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a magnifying glass over a document with one line highlighted. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Myths that waste your time
segments.narration: A few myths to drop. Myth: you need to carry a balance to build credit. False. Paying in full every month builds credit just as well, and you pay zero interest. Myth: checking your score hurts it. False. Your own checks are soft inquiries. Myth: your income affects your score. It doesn't. Income isn't in your credit report, though lenders may ask for it separately. Myth: closing a card always helps. Usually it doesn't, because you lose available credit and possibly account age. And myth: you need to pay a company to fix your credit. You don't. Disputing errors is free, and the habits that raise your score, on-time payments and low balances, are free too.
segments.on_screen_text: Myths: carry a balance, checking hurts
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a few speech bubbles with crossed-out question marks. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Let's recap. Your report is the record, and your score is the math. Payment history is about thirty-five percent, and amounts owed are about thirty percent, so autopay every minimum and keep card balances low, ideally under thirty percent of your limits. Account age, new credit and mix make up the rest and move slowly. To build from zero, use a secured card or credit-builder loan responsibly. To recover, get current, pay down balances and give it time. And check your reports for free at AnnualCreditReport dot com, disputing any errors yourself. Our full guide to how credit scores work is in the description, along with our comparison of credit-builder cards if you're starting from scratch.

script.title: How to Start Investing With $100 a Month (Beginner's Guide)
script.hook: $100 a month for 30 years at a hypothetical 7% is about $122,000. Here's exactly how to start.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: You don't need thousands of dollars to start investing. Most brokerages let you start with very little, and many let you buy fractions of a share. In this video we'll go through exactly how to start with a hundred dollars a month: what to do before you invest, which account to open first, what to actually buy, why fees matter so much, and how to automate the whole thing so you don't have to think about it. We'll also look at a hypothetical example. A hundred dollars a month, at an average seven percent return, for thirty years, comes to about a hundred and twenty-two thousand dollars. That's not a promise. Investing involves risk, and real returns go up and down. But it shows why starting early, even small, matters so much.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. the small round green piggy bank mascot with big eyes planting a small seed in a pot with a coin-shaped leaf. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Before you invest
segments.narration: Before you invest your first dollar, check three things. One: are you getting your full 401(k) match at work? If your employer matches contributions, that's often an instant fifty or one hundred percent return on that money, which is very hard to beat. Contribute at least enough to get the full match. Two: do you have high-interest debt? If you have a credit card at twenty-four percent, every dollar you pay down saves you a sure twenty-four percent in interest, and investments are never certain. So high-rate debt usually comes first. Three: do you have a starter emergency fund? Even five hundred to a thousand dollars means a surprise expense won't force you to sell investments at a bad time. Got those three? You're ready.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. three stepping stones leading to a small tree. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Which account first
segments.narration: Next, where should your hundred dollars go? Think of an account as a container, and the investments as what you put inside it. If you're already getting your 401(k) match, a common next step is a Roth IRA. You put in money you've already paid tax on, it can grow, and qualified withdrawals in retirement are tax-free. There are income limits and an annual contribution limit, so check the IRS page for this year's numbers. If you want money you can use before retirement, a regular taxable brokerage account works too, with no contribution limits but no special tax breaks. Many beginners do both over time. We have a full video comparing Roth and traditional IRAs, and a guide on where to open a Roth IRA, both linked below.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. two simple containers, one with a small leaf symbol, one plain. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: What to buy: index funds
segments.narration: Now, what goes inside the container? For most beginners, the simple answer is a broad, low-cost index fund. An index fund holds a small piece of many companies at once, like the five hundred large US companies in the S and P five hundred, or the whole US stock market, or the whole world. Instead of trying to pick the winning company, you own a little of all of them. That spreads out your risk, and historically, broad index funds have outperformed most professional fund managers over long periods, mostly because they're so cheap. Another simple option is a target-date fund. You pick the fund with the year closest to when you'll retire, and it automatically holds a mix of stocks and bonds, getting more conservative as that year gets closer. One fund, done.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a basket holding many tiny different-shaped building blocks. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: What $100 a month can become
segments.narration: Let's look at the hypothetical math. If you invest a hundred dollars a month and earn an average of seven percent a year, here's roughly what you'd have. After ten years, about seventeen thousand three hundred dollars, from twelve thousand you put in. After twenty years, about fifty-two thousand, from twenty-four thousand put in. After thirty years, about a hundred and twenty-two thousand, from thirty-six thousand put in. Notice how the growth speeds up. In the last ten years, the account grows by about seventy thousand dollars. That's compounding: your returns start earning returns. Important reminder: real markets don't give you seven percent every year. Some years are up twenty, some are down twenty or more. This is an illustration, not a forecast. But the pattern is the point. Time does most of the work.

segments.heading: Why fees matter
segments.narration: Fees are the one thing in investing you actually control, and they matter more than they look. Funds charge an annual fee called an expense ratio. A broad index fund might charge three hundredths of a percent. Some actively managed funds charge one percent or more. One percent sounds tiny. But using the same hypothetical, a hundred a month for thirty years, a fund that charges three hundredths of a percent would leave you with about a hundred and twenty-one thousand. A fund that charges one percent would leave you with about a hundred thousand. That's a difference of around twenty thousand dollars, just from fees. So before you buy any fund, look up its expense ratio. We have a full explainer on expense ratios linked below.

segments.heading: Step by step: getting started
segments.narration: Here's how to actually do it. Step one: pick a brokerage. Look for no account minimum, no trading fees on the funds you want, fractional shares, and automatic investing. We compare beginner options on our site. Step two: open the account, a Roth IRA or a regular brokerage account. You'll need your Social Security number and bank details, and it takes about fifteen minutes. Step three: link your checking account and set up an automatic transfer of a hundred dollars a month, the day after payday. Step four: set up automatic investing into your chosen fund, like a total market index fund or a target-date fund. This is the step people miss. Money sitting in the account as cash isn't invested. Step five: don't touch it. Check once a month, not once a day.

segments.heading: When the market drops
segments.narration: At some point, your investments will drop, maybe ten percent, maybe much more. This is normal and expected. It's not a sign you did something wrong. The biggest mistake beginners make is panic-selling during a drop. Selling turns a temporary dip into a permanent loss, and then you have to guess when to buy back in. If you're investing for decades, drops can actually work in your favor, because your automatic hundred dollars buys more shares when prices are lower. So decide now, before it happens, what you'll do. Write it down: when the market drops twenty percent, I keep my automatic investments running. And if you can't stand the swings, it might be a sign you need a more conservative mix, like a target-date fund with more bonds.

Investing your emergency fund. That money needs to be safe and available. Checking your account every day. It makes normal swings feel scary. And stopping your contributions after a drop. That's exactly when steady investing helps the most. Avoid these, and you're ahead of most people.

script.title: Roth vs Traditional IRA: Which One Should You Pick?
script.hook: Roth or traditional? $1,000 in each, same 20% tax rate, and they end up exactly equal. So here's what decides it.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: Roth or traditional? It's one of the most common questions people ask when they start saving for retirement, and the internet makes it sound much more complicated than it is. Here's the short version. A traditional IRA usually means you skip tax now and pay it later. A Roth IRA means you pay tax now and skip it later. That's the core difference. In this video, we'll run a simple example with a thousand dollars that shows why the two can end up exactly equal, and then the one question that breaks the tie. Then we'll cover the rules that actually matter: contribution limits, income limits, and the surprisingly flexible way Roth contributions can be withdrawn. This is general education, not tax advice, so check the details for your own situation.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. the small round green piggy bank mascot with big eyes holding two envelopes, one marked with a small sun, one with a moon. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: How each one works
segments.narration: Let's define them properly. With a traditional IRA, your contributions may be tax-deductible, which lowers your taxable income this year. The money grows without yearly taxes, and when you withdraw in retirement, the withdrawals are taxed as ordinary income. Whether you can deduct your contribution depends on your income and whether you or your spouse have a retirement plan at work. With a Roth IRA, you contribute money you've already paid tax on. There's no deduction today. But the money grows, and qualified withdrawals in retirement, generally after age fifty-nine and a half and once the account has been open at least five years, are completely tax-free. Both have the same annual contribution limit, and that limit is shared, so it's the total across all your IRAs. Check the IRS site for this year's number.
segments.on_screen_text: Traditional: deduct now. Roth: tax-free later.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. two simple jars, one with a coin entering, one with a coin leaving. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The $1,000 example
segments.narration: Here's the example that makes it click. Say you have a thousand dollars of income to put toward retirement, and your tax rate is twenty percent, both now and in retirement. With a traditional IRA, you contribute the full thousand pre-tax. Say it grows four times over the years, to four thousand. When you withdraw, you pay twenty percent tax, so you keep thirty-two hundred. With a Roth IRA, you pay twenty percent tax first, so only eight hundred goes in. It grows four times, to thirty-two hundred, and you withdraw it all tax-free. Thirty-two hundred. Exactly the same. That's the key insight. When your tax rate is the same now and later, Roth and traditional end up equal. So the whole decision comes down to one thing: will your tax rate be higher or lower later?
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. two equal stacks of coins on a balanced scale. No text, no logos, no real people.

chart.title: $1,000 of income, 20% tax now and later

segments.heading: The one question
segments.narration: So here's the one question. Do you expect your tax rate to be higher now, or higher in retirement? If your tax rate is lower now than you expect it to be later, Roth usually wins, because you pay tax at today's lower rate. This is common for people early in their careers, in their first jobs, or in a lower income year, like after a job change or during school. If your tax rate is higher now than you expect later, traditional usually wins, because you take the deduction at today's higher rate and pay tax later at a lower one. This is more common for people at their peak earning years. Nobody knows future tax rates for sure. But if you're young and just starting out, many people lean Roth.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a seesaw with a small coin on one end and a bigger coin on the other. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Rules that matter: limits
segments.narration: A few rules to know. The annual contribution limit applies to all your IRAs combined, and people fifty and older can contribute a bit more as a catch-up. You also need earned income, like wages or self-employment income, at least equal to what you contribute. Roth IRAs have income limits. If your income is above a certain level, the amount you can contribute directly is reduced, and eventually phased out. Traditional IRAs don't have an income limit to contribute, but the deduction can be limited if you have a workplace plan. These numbers change, often every year, so we're not putting them on screen as if they're permanent. Check the IRS pages linked in the description for the current limits before you contribute.
segments.on_screen_text: Check this year's limits at IRS.gov
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a small ruler and a calendar next to a jar. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The Roth flexibility
segments.narration: Here's a Roth feature that surprises a lot of people. Your contributions to a Roth IRA, the money you put in, can generally be withdrawn at any time, without tax or penalty. It's the earnings that have rules. Withdraw earnings before age fifty-nine and a half, or before the account has been open five years, and you may owe tax and a ten percent penalty, with some exceptions. That flexibility makes a Roth a little less scary for people who worry about locking money away. But be careful. A Roth is not a good emergency fund. Every dollar you withdraw is a dollar that stops growing, and you can't simply put it back later beyond the annual limit. Think of it as a backup, not a plan. Keep your emergency fund separate.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a jar with a small door at the bottom, a few coins next to it. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Roth 401(k) vs traditional 401(k)
segments.narration: The same idea applies at work. Many employers offer both a traditional 401(k) and a Roth 401(k). Traditional contributions lower your taxable income now; Roth contributions are after tax and qualified withdrawals are tax-free later. The same one question applies: is your tax rate likely higher now or later? A few differences from IRAs. 401(k) contribution limits are much higher than IRA limits. Roth 401(k)s don't have the income limits that Roth IRAs do. And employer matching contributions have traditionally gone in pre-tax, though newer rules let some plans offer Roth matches. Whatever you choose, the most important thing is to contribute at least enough to get the full match. That matters more than the Roth versus traditional choice.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. an office building with two doors and a small sign of a coin. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Can't decide? Split it.
segments.narration: If you really can't decide, you can split. Put some money in Roth and some in traditional. This gives you what's called tax diversification. In retirement, you'll have some money that's taxed when you take it out, and some that isn't, which gives you flexibility to manage your taxes year by year. For example, you might use a traditional 401(k) at work to get the match and lower today's taxes, and a Roth IRA on the side. Or split your 401(k) contributions half and half. There's no penalty for having both. And don't let this decision stop you from starting. The difference between Roth and traditional is usually much smaller than the difference between saving and not saving.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. two small plants growing side by side in one window box. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Mistakes to avoid
segments.narration: A few IRA mistakes to avoid. One: putting money in and never investing it. When you contribute to an IRA, the money often lands as cash inside the account. You still need to choose an investment, like a target-date fund or a broad index fund, or it just sits there. Two: contributing more than the limit, or contributing to a Roth when your income is over the limit. Excess contributions can trigger a six percent penalty for each year they stay in the account, so if it happens, contact your provider to fix it. Three: missing the deadline. You can usually make contributions for a given tax year until the tax filing deadline the following spring, generally in mid-April, so it's not too late in January. Four: overthinking it for months. Picking either account and starting this year beats waiting for the perfect answer. You can always change your approach next year.
segments.on_screen_text: Invest it. Mind the limit. Don't wait.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a short checklist with four ticks next to a small jar. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Let's recap. Traditional means a possible deduction now, taxes later. Roth means taxes now, qualified withdrawals tax-free later. When your tax rate is the same now and later, they come out equal, like our thousand dollar example where both ended at thirty-two hundred. So the one question is: will your tax rate be higher now or later? Lower now, lean Roth. Higher now, lean traditional. Unsure, split. Check the current contribution and income limits on the IRS site. Remember Roth contributions can be withdrawn, but keep a separate emergency fund. And always grab your full 401(k) match first. Our full Roth versus traditional guide and where to open a Roth IRA are linked below. This is education, not tax advice.

script.title: 401(k) Match Explained: Don't Leave Free Money on the Table
script.hook: On a $50,000 salary, a typical match is $1,500 a year. Here's how to make sure you get every dollar.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: If your job offers a 401(k) match and you're not getting all of it, you're turning down part of your pay. It's one of the few times in personal finance where you get free money just for showing up. But match formulas are written in a confusing way, like fifty percent up to six percent, and a lot of people either contribute too little or don't realize the money isn't fully theirs yet. In this video, we'll translate match formulas into real dollars using a fictional fifty thousand dollar salary, show what it actually costs from each paycheck, explain vesting, and cover what to invest in once the money is in there. By the end, you'll know exactly what number to set in your benefits portal.
segments.on_screen_text: Your match = part of your pay
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. the small round green piggy bank mascot with big eyes holding a small gift box with a coin on top. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: What a 401(k) is
segments.narration: A 401(k) is a retirement account through your employer. Money comes out of your paycheck automatically and gets invested. With a traditional 401(k), contributions come out before income tax, which lowers your taxable income today, and you pay tax when you withdraw in retirement. Many plans also offer a Roth 401(k), where you contribute after tax and qualified withdrawals later are tax-free. The annual contribution limit for a 401(k) is much higher than for an IRA, and it changes most years, so check the current number on the IRS site. The match is extra money your employer adds based on what you contribute. If you contribute nothing, you usually get no match at all. That's the part people miss.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a paycheck with a small slice flowing into a growing plant pot. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Match formula 1: 50% up to 6%
segments.narration: Let's decode the most common formula: fifty percent match up to six percent of salary. It means your employer adds fifty cents for every dollar you contribute, on the first six percent of your pay. With a fifty thousand dollar salary, six percent is three thousand dollars a year. Your employer adds half of that: fifteen hundred dollars. If you only contribute three percent, fifteen hundred dollars, your employer adds seven fifty. You just left seven hundred and fifty dollars of free money behind. If you contribute ten percent, the match is still fifteen hundred, because the match stops at six percent. Your extra contributions are still good for your retirement, they just don't get matched. So the magic number for this formula is six percent.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a simple bar split into a filled part and a matching smaller bar. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Match formula 2: 100% up to 4%
segments.narration: Another common formula: one hundred percent match up to four percent. Your employer matches dollar for dollar on the first four percent of your salary. On fifty thousand, four percent is two thousand dollars, and your employer adds another two thousand. That's an instant one hundred percent return on that money before it's even invested. The magic number here is four percent. Some companies use tiers, like one hundred percent on the first three percent and fifty percent on the next two. Whatever your formula, the question is always the same: what's the smallest contribution that gets the full match? You can find your plan's formula in your benefits portal, the plan's summary documents, or by asking HR. Write that percentage down. It's the most important number in your plan.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a key labelled with a percent sign next to a small lock. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: What it costs per paycheck
segments.narration: Here's the part that makes it easier to say yes. Contributing six percent of a fifty thousand dollar salary is three thousand dollars a year. If you're paid every two weeks, that's twenty-six paychecks, so about one hundred and fifteen dollars per paycheck. But because traditional contributions come out before income tax, your take-home pay drops by less than that. In a twelve percent federal tax bracket, it might be closer to a hundred dollars per paycheck, depending on your state taxes. So in our example, you give up roughly a hundred dollars per paycheck, and you get a hundred and fifteen invested, plus fifteen hundred a year from your employer. If six percent feels impossible right now, start with whatever you can, and increase it by one percent every time you get a raise.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a small paycheck stub with a slice taken out, a smaller slice returned. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Vesting: when the match becomes yours
segments.narration: Now the fine print. Money you contribute from your paycheck is always one hundred percent yours. But your employer's match may come with a vesting schedule, which means you earn ownership of it over time. With cliff vesting, you own zero percent of the match until a set date, then all of it at once, and that can be up to three years. With graded vesting, you own a bit more each year, reaching full ownership by year six at the latest. Some employers vest immediately. Why does this matter? If you're thinking about leaving a job, check your vested balance first. If you're a couple of months from a vesting date, it might be worth waiting, or negotiating with your new employer to cover what you'd lose.
segments.on_screen_text: Your money: always yours. Match: may vest.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a small staircase with a coin on each step, getting fuller. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: What to invest in
segments.narration: Here's a mistake that's more common than you'd think: money goes into the 401(k), but it's sitting in a cash or money market option, not really invested. Log in and check what your contributions are actually buying. Many plans default to a target-date fund, which holds a mix of stocks and bonds based on the year you'll retire. For many people, that's a reasonable, simple choice. If your plan has a low-cost index fund, like an S and P five hundred or total market fund, that's another common pick. Look at each fund's expense ratio. Some 401(k) funds charge one percent or more, and over decades that adds up to a lot. If your plan's choices are expensive, still get the match, then consider putting extra savings into an IRA where you choose the funds.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a magnifying glass over a small basket of building blocks. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Changing jobs
segments.narration: When you leave a job, your vested 401(k) money doesn't disappear. You usually have a few options. Leave it in the old plan, if the plan allows it. Roll it into your new employer's 401(k). Or roll it into an IRA, where you have more control over the investments. What you generally want to avoid is cashing it out. If you take the money as cash before retirement age, you'll usually owe income tax plus a ten percent early withdrawal penalty, with some exceptions, and you lose years of growth. If you do a rollover, ask for a direct rollover, where the money goes straight from one account to the other. That avoids withholding headaches. And keep a list of every old plan, so nothing gets lost over the years.
segments.on_screen_text: Roll it over. Don't cash it out.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a coin rolling along a path from one building to another. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Common mistakes
segments.narration: Quick list of 401(k) mistakes. Not contributing enough to get the full match. Assuming your money is invested when it's sitting in cash. Ignoring fund fees. Cashing out when you change jobs. Forgetting to update your beneficiary. And borrowing from your 401(k) for non-emergencies. A 401(k) loan might look cheap, but if you leave your job, the balance may be due quickly, and the money you borrowed misses out on growth. One more: forgetting to increase contributions. Many plans offer automatic escalation, which raises your contribution by one percent each year. Turn it on once, and your savings rate grows without you having to remember.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a short checklist with five ticks next to a growing plant. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Let's recap. A 401(k) match is part of your pay, and you usually only get it if you contribute. Translate your formula into dollars. With fifty percent up to six percent on fifty thousand, contribute six percent and get fifteen hundred a year. With one hundred percent up to four percent, contribute four percent and get two thousand. Check your vesting schedule before you leave a job. Make sure your money is actually invested, often in a target-date or low-cost index fund, and watch the fees. When you change jobs, roll it over rather than cashing out. And turn on automatic escalation if your plan has it. Our full 401(k) match guide and expense ratio explainer are linked in the description.
